question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: Ensemble suggests a high likelihood (88%) of increasing the settlement qualifying period to 10 years, with momentum indicated by official proposals and analyses pointing to implementation around spring 2026.
Adversarial objections identify real procedural, legal, and political hurdles that could delay enactment or alter retrospective rules, representing credible downside risk.
Threshold analysis indicates the 10-year baseline is plausible by May 2026, but final enactment remains contingent on legislation and rulemaking, introducing substantial uncertainty.
Calibrated probability modestly downweights the ensemble given the concrete implementation uncertainties, while still maintaining a high-likelihood view.

justification.critique_assessment: Valid; objections describe real and non-trivial risks to timely enactment and retrospective applicability.
justification.adjustment: Downshift from 0.88 to 0.82 to reflect credible procedural delays and transitional-rule uncertainties; range accommodates possible timing variations while preserving the overall high-likelihood stance.

forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration policy base rate: the typical baseline path to settlement has been a fixed 5-year residence period for most routes, which is the reference point targeted for change under the Earned Settlement reforms.

sources.claim: The default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from the current 5 years to 10 years, with options for longer or shorter adjustments based on contributions and other factors.

IPPR analyzes the earned settlement proposal, estimating around 1.35 million people on routes to settlement could face a longer default qualifying period (10 years for many, 15 years for some) under the reforms.

Financial Times reports the reforms to base the path to settlement on a 10-year baseline for most migrants, with high earners and certain categories seeing shorter paths, and others longer depending on earnings and contributions.
KPMG flash alert notes the reforms aim to begin implementing from April 2026, with a 10-year baseline as a central element of the earned settlement plan.
Migration Observatory summarizes that the proposal would raise the standard waiting period from 5 to 10 years (with exceptions), reflecting expert consensus on the policy direction.
Persistent coverage indicates the 10-year baseline is part of the reforms, with implementation hoped for starting around April 2026 if adopted.
GOV.UK explains the Earned Settlement model and states the default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from 5 years to 10 years, with possible reductions based on contributions.
GOV.UK guidance confirms a 10-year continuous residence requirement as the standard qualifying period for settlement via the Long Residence route.
House of Commons Library summary notes that post-2025 immigration changes propose a baseline 10-year qualifying period for many migrants, with some faster or slower paths depending on circumstances.

House of Commons Library reports on petitions opposing the 10-year ILR proposal and notes the government states the Earned Settlement consultation will decide whether the change applies to people already in the UK.
UK Employment Hub reports the Home Office intends to raise the standard qualifying period to 10 years under Earned Settlement, with potential implementation as early as April 2026.
Law firm notes the consultation closes February 12, 2026 and that changes may take effect as soon as April 2026.

Guardian reporting highlights IPPR concerns about extended waiting periods for settled status for children under the proposed reforms, illustrating debate and perceived risk in implementation timelines.

The government published an open consultation on 'earned settlement' proposing to increase the standard qualifying period for settlement from five to ten years, with a time-adjustment model for reductions or extensions.
The 'A Fairer Pathway to Settlement' documents indicate the standard qualifying period will be ten years and describe the four-pillar time-adjustment framework to adjust the baseline.
House of Commons Library briefing notes note that the government announced more details on 20 November 2025, with a baseline ten-year qualifying period for settlement.
The consultation closed on 12 February 2026; implementation dates are expected to be staggered starting in April 2026.
Guardian reporting notes the government's plan to extend the waiting period for permanent settlement from five to ten years as part of the immigration reforms.

synthesis: The policy direction strongly favors a 10-year baseline, with credible signals of near-term rollout. However, procedural and retrospective uncertainties create meaningful risk of delay beyond May 2026, justifying a slight downshift from the ensemble mean to about 0.82 with a broad but plausible range.
